learn.what: Two pointers is a technique where two indexes move through a sequence according to a useful rule instead of repeatedly scanning the same elements.
recognize: The input is sorted or can be sorted.
You need to find a pair or combination.
You compare values from two ends.
You need to process or compact elements efficiently.
learn.oppositeDirection: One pointer starts on the left and another on the right. Move one of them based on the condition you are trying to satisfy.
learn.sameDirection: Two pointers can move forward together. One may read elements while another tracks a position to place or keep a valid value.
mistakes: Using two pointers when the problem does not provide the right structure.
Ignoring whether sorting changes the problem.

problems.why: Practice opposite-direction pointers on sorted input.

problems.why: Apply two-pointer reasoning to a more advanced optimization problem.

learn.what: Sliding Window maintains a moving range over an array or string so that information from the previous range can be reused.
recognize: The problem asks about a contiguous subarray or substring.
You need a maximum, minimum, count or length over a moving range.
The current range can expand or shrink.
learn.oppositeDirection: Sliding Window usually does not use opposite-direction pointers. The left and right boundaries normally move forward.
learn.sameDirection: The right pointer expands the window and the left pointer shrinks it when the window becomes invalid.
mistakes: Forgetting to remove the left element.
Confusing a substring/subarray with a subsequence.

problems.why: Master variable windows with multiple frequency constraints.

learn.what: Binary Search repeatedly cuts a sorted or monotonic search space in half.
recognize: There is a monotonic yes/no condition.
You need to find a boundary or exact position.
A linear search would repeatedly examine too many values.
learn.oppositeDirection: Left and right boundaries represent the current search space.
learn.sameDirection: The search boundaries shrink toward the answer based on the middle value.
mistakes: Using binary search without a sorted or monotonic property.

problems.why: Apply binary-search partition reasoning to two arrays.
